tip: 'Le sienta bien' works like 'gustar': 'ese color' is the subject and 'le' marks the person – literally 'that color sits well to her'.
Spanish has no everyday verb 'to feed' – you 'give of eating': 'diste de comer al perro' = you gave the dog (something) to eat.
'Está enferma desde el lunes' uses plain present where English needs 'has been.' Spanish logic: she is sick right now, and 'desde' just points back to when it started.
No 'on' needed: 'El lunes empiezo' – the article alone means 'on Monday'. Singular 'el lunes' = this Monday; plural 'los lunes' = every Monday.
After 'antes de' comes a bare infinitive: 'antes de salir', literally 'before to-go-out.' English 'before leaving' tempts you toward a gerund Spanish never uses here.
In 'nos queda una semana', the week is the subject – 'a week remains to us.' That's why the verb is 'queda': 'quedar' agrees with what's left, not with who has it.
'¿Qué es la dirección?' would ask what an address IS – a definition. To pick out a specific one, Spanish switches to 'cuál es la dirección'.
'Parecerse' = to resemble each other. Reciprocal: 'se parecen' = they look alike; 'nos parecemos' = we look alike.
'Salir' here isn't 'to leave' – 'sale barato' means the deal 'comes out' cheap, like a bill totaling up. 'Me' marks who it's cheap for: buying online comes out cheaper for me.
English has no verb for 'take time' – Spanish does: 'tardar'. '¿Cuánto tardarás en preparar...?' = how long will you take? And it's always 'tardar en' + infinitive.
'Coja' (from 'coger', to take) is normal in Spain – but 'coger' is crude slang in much of Latin America. There, say 'tomar un taxi' instead.
'Tardar' takes 'en' where English says 'take TO': 'tardas en llegar'. Learn it as one chunk – 'tardar en' + infinitive – and you'll never be tempted to translate that 'to' as 'a'.
This 'para' isn't the preposition 'for' – it's the verb 'parar': 'el autobús para', the bus stops. A subject sitting right before 'para' is your clue something is stopping.
'Vas a hacer': conjugated 'ir' + 'a' + bare verb. That little 'a' is the glue – skip it and the sentence breaks. Spaniards use this far more than actual future-tense endings.
'Faltar': 'nos falta' – we're missing/lacking. Works like 'gustar'.
'Quedar': 'nos quedan' – we have... left. Plural agrees with 'dos días'.
'Estar' for temporary states and taste: 'están sosas' = they taste bland. Compare: 'son buenas' (generally good) vs 'están buenas' (taste good now).
'Hay que + infinitive' = one must / you have to (impersonal obligation). 'Hay que barrer' = you have to sweep. Different from 'tener que' (personal).
'En quien' = in whom. After prepositions, use 'quien' for people: 'el compañero en quien confío' = the colleague I trust in.
'Me gusta ducharme' – when 'gustar' is followed by an infinitive, use singular 'gusta' (not 'gustan'). The infinitive acts as the subject.
You won't 'give your arm to be twisted': 'dar mi brazo a torcer' pictures losing an arm-wrestle. Refusing to = standing firm, not giving in.
Physical descriptions with 'tener': 'tiene los ojos verdes' = she has green eyes. Spanish uses the article 'los' with body parts.
'Sonar' = to ring a bell / sound familiar. 'Me suena' = it sounds familiar to me. Uses a 'gustar'-like construction.
'Doler' works like 'gustar': the body part is the subject. 'Me duele la cabeza' = My head hurts (lit. the head hurts to me). Plural: 'me duelen los pies.'
'El día' is masculine – an exception. 'Buenos días' (good days) shows the masculine adjective form.
'La radio' – feminine because it's short for 'la radioemisora.' Gender follows the full word.
In Spanish, normally no article before professions: 'Soy ingeniero' (not 'Soy un ingeniero').
'Costar': 'le cuesta' – it's hard for him/her. Works like 'gustar'.
'Toca' here isn't 'touch' – 'nos toca' means 'it falls to us': it's our turn. The 'a nosotros' at the end doubles down: it's OUR turn to pay, nobody else's.
'Encantar' works like 'gustar': the thing loved is the subject. 'Me encantó' = it enchanted me.
